title: The treasure under the bridge
hookLine: Isaac of Kraków travels to Prague for a dreamed treasure and learns it's under his own stove (Hasidic tale)

lines: THE THING THAT WILL FIX EVERYTHING.
cards: Somewhere out there is the thing that will fix everything. The better city. The better job.
The retreat in the mountains. The person who finally gets you. A lot of life goes into planning the trip to go and get it.
There's a Hasidic tale about a man who actually made that trip: Isaac, the son of Yekel, a poor, devout man in Kraków, in Poland.
Night after night, he dreams the same dream: go to Prague, and under the bridge that leads to the king's castle, you'll find a treasure. The third time he has the dream, he packs a bag.

teach.b: It's a long walk from Kraków to Prague. When Isaac gets there, he finds the bridge, guarded by soldiers day and night, and he doesn't dare dig.
So every day he comes back and circles it, until the captain of the guard notices and asks, kindly enough, what he's looking for. Isaac, having nothing to lose, tells him about the dream.
And the captain laughs. You walked all this way because of a dream? If I believed in dreams, I'd have gone to Kraków long ago!
I keep dreaming there's a treasure under the stove of some Jew called Isaac, son of Yekel.
Imagine walking all that way, where half the men are called Isaac and the other half Yekel!
Isaac thanks him, walks all the way home, digs under his own stove, and finds the treasure. Tradition says he used it to build a synagogue, and in Kraków there is still one known by his name.
Martin Buber's collection records Rabbi Simcha Bunim, the teacher of the two pockets, telling this story to young men who came to him for the first time.
He'd add something like: there's something you can't find anywhere in the world, not even with a great teacher, but there is a place where you can find it.

The same story turns up in other homes too: in the Thousand and One Nights and in Rumi, it's a man of Baghdad who dreams of Cairo. But notice: Isaac still had to make the journey. The trip didn't hold the treasure.
It showed him where it had been all along.

how: The tale of Isaac of Kraków is told in Hasidic teaching about finding what's sacred close to home, and the old synagogue in Kraków's Kazimierz district that bears the name of Isaac son of Jacob is often linked to it.

o: a blessing said over a newly built home
a long journey taken because of a dream
treasure, or a store of something precious

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: dreamed of a treasure in Prague
dreamed of a stove in Kraków

s: Isaac found the treasure under the bridge in Prague
it was under his own stove. the captain's dream told him where.
a similar tale appears in the Thousand and One Nights and in Rumi
there it's a man of Baghdad who dreams of a treasure in Cairo.
the story says Isaac's trip was wasted
he had to make the journey to learn where the treasure had been all along.

games.q: you're Isaac. you've walked to Prague, and the captain laughs: he dreams of treasure under the stove of a man called Isaac, son of Yekel, in Kraków. what do you do?
o: thank him, go home, and dig under your stove.
games.why: he walks home, digs under his own stove, and finds the treasure. tradition says he built a synagogue with it.

practice: Picture your home, or wherever you live right now, and walk through it slowly, room by room, the way Isaac walked home.
Look for something good you've stopped seeing: a person, a window with light, a chair that holds you, a cup you love, a plant still alive despite you. Stop there, and dig a little.

wordCard.voice: otzar, Hebrew for treasure. Isaac walked all the way to Prague for his, and learned it was under his own stove.

orig.note: Hebrew, otzar: treasure, or a treasury.

carryVoice: Your line: it was under the stove. Sometimes the treasure is closer than the trip. See you tomorrow.
